evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Direct comparative evidence under a substantially matched implementation foundation. The study tests whether workflow decomposition and role separation, rather than different tools or engineering stacks, change end-to-end software-development performance. It supports a conditional advantage for a two-agent Developer-Tester workflow, while also showing that extra agents and extra decomposition can be harmful.
evidence_notes.research_design: Controlled empirical study on E2EDevBench, a benchmark of 50 recent PyPI projects sampled across 2024-Q1 through 2025-Q1. Three workflows share a SWE-Agent foundation: one all-purpose agent (SDAgent-Single), sequential Developer-Tester agents (SDAgent-DT), and sequential Designer-Developer-Tester agents (SDAgent-DDT). Each was run with Gemini-2.5-Pro and Gemini-2.5-Flash at temperature 0.2 and a 200-step maximum. Evaluation combines migrated original tests with three independent binary requirement judgments; unanimous judgments determine implementation status. The paper also analyzes three independent Gemini-2.5-Pro runs and manually classifies 1,000 unimplemented requirements.

held_constant: All three workflows use the same SWE-Agent foundation, mature toolset, environment interaction capabilities, benchmark, and evaluation pipeline.
Within each model comparison, the underlying model, temperature, and maximum step allowance are held constant.
Development agents receive requirements rather than reference tests or code skeletons; a separate migration agent adapts tests only after development.
omitted_or_confounded: The architecture study is limited to two Gemini variants and Python package development; no cross-family model replication is reported.
The multi-agent workflows are simplified to sequential handoffs, so results do not test richer debate, parallelism, or dynamic delegation.
Actual token use, number of steps, generated code size, and cost differ substantially, so the comparison is not budget-matched even though all runs share a 200-step ceiling.
No inferential significance test or confidence interval is reported for the workflow-level implementation-rate differences.
Gemini-2.5-Pro is also used for dataset annotation, test migration, and judging, creating a possible same-model evaluation affinity that is not separately controlled.
Role instructions necessarily differ across workflows; the paper matches the engineering foundation and tools, not literal prompts or context trajectories.

headline_results.finding: Table 3 reports mean requirement implementation rates of 49.48% for SDAgent-DT, 45.72% for SDAgent-Single, and 27.71% for SDAgent-DDT. With Gemini-2.5-Pro specifically, DT reaches 53.50%, versus 42.97% for Single and 32.79% for DDT. With Flash, however, Single reaches 48.46% and DT 45.47%, a negative result against any universal multi-agent advantage.

The top configuration, SDAgent-DT plus Gemini-2.5-Pro, averages 5.24 million sent tokens, 49.65 thousand generated tokens, and an estimated $7.05 per project while implementing only 53.50% of requirements.

Migrated tests expose defects missed by agent-written tests: pass rate is 59.66% for extended tests versus 93.14% for original tests; combining them increases average covered lines by 20.22% and covered branches by 26.79%.

Failure attribution assigns 55.8% of issues to planning, 38.6% to execution, and 5.7% to verification. Requirement omission is 27.9%, misinterpretation 22.2%, architectural design flaws 5.6%, dependent feature failures 21.0%, and inadequate verification 5.7%.

The authors attribute DT's advantage to separating implementation from later testing, which reduces reactive local-fixing loops and context loss. They attribute DDT's poor performance to flawed design plans becoming authoritative and propagating downstream. These mechanisms are inferred from trajectory patterns rather than isolated by component ablation.
Across three Pro runs, DT has 796 requirements fulfilled in all runs and 526 fulfilled in only one run, supporting best-of-N as a possible stability method but at full-run computational cost.

limitations: The prose on page 7 mistakenly calls SDAgent-Single the 49.48% configuration, while Table 3 assigns 49.48% to SDAgent-DT; the table and surrounding conclusion support the latter reading.
Table 4 gives Incomplete Implementation as 18.1%, while the accompanying page-9 prose says 21.7%; the discrepancy is unresolved in the paper.
About half of the requirements remain unmet even in the best configuration, and the evaluation does not establish production maintainability, security, or human acceptance.
Three stochastic runs are analyzed only for Gemini-2.5-Pro, and best-of-N feasibility is not evaluated under a fixed cost budget.
The controlled benchmark improves realism but remains a 50-project Python sample rather than a multi-language industrial deployment study.
future_work: Improve requirement comprehension, complete task decomposition, and validation before and during implementation.
Develop rigorous self-verification that uses stronger tests and requirement-level checks.
Optimize workflow orchestration and cost-effective aggregation instead of adding roles indiscriminately.
Replace simplistic self-submission conditions that may cause capable models to terminate prematurely.
combinable_methods: A Developer-Tester separation on top of a shared capable tool interface.
Independent post-development test migration plus requirement-by-requirement verification.
Multiple stochastic runs with selective aggregation, provided marginal gains are evaluated against cost.
Requirement traceability and explicit completion gates to prevent omission and premature submission.

quotes.text: Using this framework, we conduct a controlled empirical study on three representative agent architectures implemented upon a unified foundation to isolate the impact of workflow design.
quotes.use: Evidence that the study intentionally controls the implementation foundation to isolate workflow architecture.

quotes.text: To isolate the influence of implementation-specific factors and facilitate a fair comparison under controlled conditions, we adopted a strategic approach: we selected the representative open-source project SWE-Agent [41] to serve as the unified foundational architecture for all our experimental agents.
quotes.use: Exact description of the principal architecture-comparison control.

quotes.text: The experimental findings reveal that the SDAgent-DT paired with the Gemini-2.5-Pro model achieved the highest requirement implementation rate of 53.50%.
quotes.use: Measured headline result for the best two-agent configuration.

quotes.text: A single -agent approach is not necessarily optimal. A well -structured division of tasks and agents can effectively reduce task complexity, whereas an inappropriate decomposition can substantially degrade agent performance.
quotes.use: Author conclusion that multi-agent value depends on decomposition quality rather than agent count.

quotes.text: The results in Table 5, clearly indicate that “Task Planning” is the primary bottleneck in current agent systems, accounting for 55.8% of all issues.
quotes.use: Measured failure analysis locating the dominant bottleneck upstream of code execution.

evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Architecture proposal and feasibility illustration, not comparative evidence. ALMAS motivates agile role specialization, model routing, compact code memory, verification, and human escalation, but it does not test whether this multi-agent design outperforms a matched single agent.
evidence_notes.research_design: Vision paper describing an agile-aligned modular architecture with Sprint, Supervisor, Summary, Control, Developer, Code, and Peer agents. The integrated prototype is illustrated on one workflow that creates a Python Streamlit stock-options application and then adds a bar-chart feature. All agents use GPT-4o in the exercise and integrate with Jira and Bitbucket. Component agents had been studied independently in prior work, but the paper supplies no end-to-end benchmark experiment.

held_constant: All agents in the illustrative integrated exercise use GPT-4o.
The framework defines modular responsibilities and common handoffs across the example workflow.
omitted_or_confounded: No single-agent, fewer-agent, or existing multi-agent baseline is run.
No matched requirements, prompts, tool-access, token budget, latency budget, or repeated trials are reported.
The one application-plus-feature demonstration has no quantitative correctness, cost, latency, security, or maintainability metrics.

Claims that task routing, summaries, and specialization reduce cost or context problems are design assertions here; their evidence resides, if anywhere, in cited component papers rather than this integrated study.

headline_results.finding: The prototype completes one Streamlit application-generation workflow and one subsequent feature augmentation using common task-management and version-control tools. This establishes feasibility only.

The proposed architecture claims benefits from assigning lightweight or advanced models by task complexity, maintaining structured code summaries, localizing code through Meta-RAG, and letting specialized development and review agents collaborate. No integrated ablation measures those contributions.

Verification includes formatting, compilation, unit tests, peer review for functionality, vulnerabilities, performance, hallucinations, formal verification, and quality; failed automated recovery escalates to a human with an action summary.
The authors explicitly defer the necessary end-to-end evaluation, so the paper cannot establish comparative performance or production readiness.

limitations: One illustrative use case cannot support causal claims about specialization, orchestration, or model routing.
The paper does not report whether generated tests passed, whether peer-review findings were repaired, or whether the feature met independently assessed requirements.
Human collaboration and escalation are specified architecturally but not evaluated with users or failure scenarios.
No reliability analysis, repeated execution, fault injection, or cost measurement is included.
future_work: Conduct end-to-end evaluations across a range of coding tasks.
Evaluate on SWE-bench and measure intermediate outcomes such as localization efficiency.
Quantify integrated behavior rather than relying on prior isolated component studies.
combinable_methods: Agile role decomposition with acceptance criteria produced before implementation.
Structured natural-language code summaries plus retrieval-based code localization for context control.
Capability- and cost-aware model routing by a supervisor.
Unit tests, peer review, vulnerability checks, and formal verification as layered gates.
Bounded automated recovery followed by human handoff with summarized action history.

quotes.text: ALMAS agents were evaluated independently in previous works, but in this paper, we outline the framework’s blueprint; detailing agent roles, interaction dynamics, and resource allocation strategies, and present a case study where an initial prototype successfully tackled a task that involved both the creation of a new application and the modification of existing code to add a new feature.
quotes.use: Scope boundary: blueprint and prototype case rather than integrated comparative evaluation.

quotes.text: The Summary Agent generates concise, structured natural-language summaries for each code unit, addressing LLM context limitations and reducing token costs.
quotes.use: Proposed memory-context and cost-control mechanism; an architectural claim in this paper.

quotes.text: Validation is built in: the Developer Agent checks code formatting, compilation, and runs unit tests to ensure correctness.
quotes.use: Specified deterministic verification layer.

quotes.text: If automated recovery fails after several attempts, control passes to a human developer with a summarized action history, ensuring resilience.
quotes.use: Specified bounded-retry and human-escalation method.

quotes.text: The necessary end-to-end evaluation will be explored more thoroughly in future.
quotes.use: Explicit admission that comparative end-to-end evidence remains absent.

evidence_notes.reason: The manifest contains neither a PDF nor a text_file for order 17, so no full-text evidence or page-anchored quotations are available.

evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Comparative evidence that explicit contracts, typed messaging, and verification-gated lifecycle control can improve one multi-agent system relative to another. It does not compare multi-agent operation with a single agent and therefore supports complementary production-hardening methods more strongly than the focal single-versus-multi hypothesis.
evidence_notes.research_design: Preliminary evaluation of SEMAP against a MetaGPT baseline on HumanEval function development, ProgramDev deployment-level development, devign100 C/C++ vulnerability detection, and vudenc100 Python vulnerability detection. Development uses a centralized five-role setup and up to five collaboration rounds; vulnerability detection uses decentralized Auditor, Critic, and Tester agents for one round. Both DeepSeek-V3-0324 and gpt-4.1-nano-2025-04-14 are tested. A separate gpt-4o-2024-08-06 judge applies the MAST failure taxonomy for under-specification, inter-agent misalignment, and verification failure.

held_constant: The same two underlying model versions and task datasets are used across baseline and SEMAP conditions.
Both conditions use the same maximum of five rounds for development and one round for vulnerability detection.
Both vulnerability-detection conditions use the same three decentralized roles.
omitted_or_confounded: The baseline is implemented in MetaGPT while SEMAP is middleware over Google's A2A infrastructure, so protocol effects are entangled with framework and implementation differences.
No single-agent LLM, domain detector, or non-agent protocol baseline is included.
The outcome is judge-classified failure count rather than functional task success, code quality, vulnerability-detection precision/recall, or production behavior.
No ablation isolates behavioral contracts, structured messaging, or lifecycle verification.
Resource overhead, token use, latency, and cost are not measured.
Artifacts were not yet released in the paper, limiting independent reproduction.

headline_results.finding: On HumanEval, total judged failures fall from 256 to 92 with GPT-4.1-nano (64.1%) and from 112 to 34 with DeepSeek-V3 (69.6%). Under-specification falls by 71.5% and 73.0%, respectively.

On ProgramDev, total failures fall from 103 to 90 with GPT-4.1-nano (12.6%) and from 67 to 29 with DeepSeek-V3 (56.7%). The wide model-dependent difference is negative evidence against assuming uniform protocol gains.
For vulnerability detection, total judged failures fall by 28.2% and 8.3% on devign100, and by 47.4% and 16.4% on vudenc100, for GPT-4.1-nano and DeepSeek-V3 respectively.
By round 5, HumanEval under-specification failures reach 2 for GPT-SEMAP and 0 for DeepSeek-SEMAP, versus 9 and 2 for their baselines; ProgramDev reaches 3 and 0, versus 3 and 3.
The authors infer that SEMAP produces more stable collaboration because baseline failures reappear after temporary drops. Component-level causality remains untested without ablation.

limitations: The experiment demonstrates protocol-versus-framework improvement, not specialized multi-agent superiority over a matched single agent.
Failure counts can assign more than one category per instance and do not directly reveal whether the final software or vulnerability label is correct.
Only two models, two development datasets, and two 100-sample vulnerability subsets are included.
The paper calls the evaluation preliminary and explicitly leaves larger datasets, longer workflows, more baselines, and ablations to future work.
future_work: Scale to larger datasets, more agents, and longer workflows.
Add single-agent LLM and domain-specific detector baselines.
Ablate contracts, messaging, and lifecycle control separately.
Measure resource overhead and support cross-agent tool use.
Add formal protocol-correctness verification and release reproducibility artifacts.
combinable_methods: Behavioral contracts specifying required input and output artifacts for each role.
Schema-typed messages with explicit sender, receiver, and payload objects.
Finite-state lifecycle control whose transitions are gated by verification outcomes.
Recovery or reassignment on failed verification rather than unconditional workflow progression.
Independent failure-taxonomy analysis across rounds to detect recurrence rather than final failure alone.

quotes.text: This paper introduces Software Engineering Multi-Agent Protocol (SEMAP), a protocol-layer methodology that instantiates three core SE design principles for multi-agent LLMs: (1) explicit behavioral contract modeling, (2) structured messaging, and (3) lifecycle-guided execution with verification
quotes.use: Definition of the three complementary protocol mechanisms.

quotes.text: The baseline system is implemented using the MetaGPT framework. For development tasks, it adopts a centralized CEO-style multi-agent architecture consisting of five agents: a CEO, a Planner, a Coder, a Reviewer, and a Tester.
quotes.use: Shows that the comparator is another multi-agent framework, not a single agent.

quotes.text: In function-level development (HumanEval), SEMAP reduces the total number of failures by 64.1% with ChatGPT (from 256 to 92) and by 69.6% with DeepSeek (from 112 to 34).
quotes.use: Measured failure-count improvement on function-level development.

quotes.text: Compared to the baseline, SEMAP not only reduces failure counts more effectively, but also exhibits a more stable downward trend across rounds, whereas baseline failures often reappear after temporary drops.
quotes.use: Round-wise stability finding, stated as the authors' interpretation of the traces.

quotes.text: To strengthen validity, future experiments will be scaled to larger datasets, agent populations, and longer workflows, and compared against more baselines, including single-agent LLMs and domain-specific detectors. Ablation studies will isolate the impact of contracts, messaging, and lifecycle control.
quotes.use: Explicitly identifies missing single-agent controls and component ablations.

evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Review-level evidence about why apparent agent gains often fail to establish production readiness. It does not empirically compare a specialized multi-agent system with a matched single agent, but it supplies an evaluation framework for making such comparisons credible and deployable.
evidence_notes.research_design: Systematic review following a stated PRISMA process over IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, arXiv, Google Scholar, and Springer for 2021-2025. The paper reports 1,247 initial records, 384 after deduplication and title/abstract screening, 95 after full-text review, then 89 eligible papers and 52 included papers: 15 primary benchmarks plus 37 supporting works. Fifteen benchmarks are compared across task structure, metrics, datasets, validity, reproducibility, and deployment gaps. Two authors independently scored five benchmarks across five rubric dimensions, agreeing exactly on 21/25 ratings (84%).

held_constant: The review applies a common deployment-gap vocabulary across 15 heterogeneous benchmarks.
Its rubric operationalizes cost transparency, safety coverage, maintainability, trajectory quality, and robustness on a common 0-5 scale.
A two-rater check covers five selected benchmarks and all five rubric dimensions.
omitted_or_confounded: No primary matched experiment compares single-agent and multi-agent architectures.
The benchmarks span incompatible domains and tasks; conclusions are comparative review judgments rather than a meta-analysis of common effect sizes.
Rubric reliability is checked on only 5 of 15 benchmarks, with disagreements resolved by discussion rather than an independently reported chance-corrected statistic.
The PRISMA narrative moves from 95 papers after full-text review to 89 eligible papers without explaining six exclusions.
The paper reports many deployment statistics from cited studies; these are secondary evidence and were not generated or independently replicated by this review.
Architecture-specific claims remain conceptual because the review does not stratify matched benchmark outcomes by single-agent versus multi-agent design.

headline_results.finding: Across the 15 reviewed benchmarks, security is absent in 15/15 primary evaluation schemes; cost is only partially represented by action counts in 2/15 and absent in 13/15; safety is partial in 1/15; robustness is partial in 3/15. The conclusion summarizes that 13/15 rely on binary success as the sole criterion and 14/15 do not measure trajectory quality.

The deployment-readiness rubric assigns SWE-bench 20% and WebArena approximately 45%; no reviewed benchmark exceeds 50%. These are author-designed rubric scores, not observed deployment success rates.

The review reports that test-pass rate and code quality correlate at r=0.31, and elsewhere reports a SWE-bench deployment sample with test-pass versus acceptance correlation r=0.43 and maintainability correlation r=0.12. These values are synthesized from cited sources rather than estimated in this review.

Outcome-only metrics cannot distinguish coherent planning from trial-and-error, efficient tool use from brute-force retries, or materially different failure modes in ReAct, Reflexion, and multi-agent architectures.

The authors argue that evaluation methodology, rather than model capability, is now the principal deployment bottleneck. The benchmark-gap counts support widespread measurement omissions, but the stronger causal formulation is a review thesis rather than an experimentally isolated result.

limitations: The review focuses on LLM-based agents; reinforcement-learning and neuro-symbolic agents are excluded.

Benchmark-selection thresholds are described differently across sections (at least 50 citations or major venue on page 11; more than 100 citations or major deployment for the 15 representatives on page 14).
The common rubric imposes expert judgments on heterogeneous domains, and only a subset receives duplicate ratings.
Several exact production claims depend on supporting citations and should not be treated as primary data from this paper.
Data availability states that no datasets were generated or analyzed, even though benchmark attributes and rubric scores are presented; no separate extraction dataset is described.
future_work: Standardize capability, environment, cost, safety, robustness, and trajectory definitions across benchmarks.
Use continuous lifecycle evaluation and versioned dynamic tasks to detect regressions and distribution drift.
Develop scalable proxies and adaptive sampling for expensive interactive evaluation.
Test transfer across task families, environments, and functionally equivalent toolsets.
Create architecture-aware protocols that fairly compare structurally different agent systems.
combinable_methods: Trajectory-level scoring of planning coherence, tool selection, retries, and error recovery.
Cost-normalized success using API cost, tokens, latency, and compute budget.
Safety-constrained scoring, adversarial cases, and runtime contract monitoring for silent failures.
Automated functional checks combined with security, maintainability, integration, and human code review.
Continuous regression evaluation under environment drift, model updates, and changing APIs.
Human-in-the-loop assessment for explanations, interaction quality, and acceptable autonomy.

quotes.text: Quantitatively, 0/15 benchmarks integrate safety or security into scoring, 0/15 include cost-efficiency metrics in their primary evaluation protocol, and 13/15 rely exclusively on binary success measures
quotes.use: Core review evidence for systematic deployment-metric omissions.

quotes.text: Exact agreement was achieved on 21 of 25 dimension-benchmark pairs (84%), with the remaining 4 cases differing by one point on the 0–5 scale.
quotes.use: Reported reliability check for the authors' deployment-gap rubric.

quotes.text: This is problematic in the case of architecture different agents where ReAct systems, Reflexion frameworks, and multi-agent architectures have different trajectory structures, which are not well represented by existing metrics.
quotes.use: Why outcome-only evaluation can obscure architecture-specific benefits and failures.

quotes.text: Empirical analysis (Table 6) reveals systematic safety evaluation gaps: 0/15 benchmarks penalize unsafe tool usage, 0/15 test adversarial robustness systematically, and only ALFWorld partially considers safety (collision detection) without integrating it into scoring.
quotes.use: Specific security, safety, and robustness gap counts.

quotes.text: The modern standards are mostly architecture-neutral and use agents as black boxes whose fitness is judged by inputoutput behaviour alone. Nevertheless, alternative agent architecture ReAct-style prompted systems, Reflexion-based self-improvement loops, or multi-agent collaborative models can have entirely new capability profiles and failure behaviour.
quotes.use: Rationale for architecture-aware matched comparisons.

evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Adjacent evidence for human-agent consensus and role-specialized discussion, but not evidence that a multi-agent system outperforms a matched single agent. The numerical accuracy experiment deliberately isolates one SEEAgent; the multi-agent portion is an uncontrolled user-perception study.
evidence_notes.research_design: Two-part evaluation. RQ1 tests a standalone SEEAgent long-term-memory component using base and project-specific QLoRA-fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct against Deep-SE, GPT2SP, and Fine-SE on four public Jira projects (DM, ME, TD, US; 4,907 total issues), preserving Fine-SE train/test splits and using MAE, MMRE, PRED(50), Wilcoxon tests, and Vargha-Delaney effect sizes. RQ2 is a human study with 12 purposively recruited practitioners. Each session uses three human developers, two GPT-4o-mini SEEAgents with front-end or back-end role prompts, and the first author as product owner on a simplified 33-story e-commerce project, followed by a 12-item Likert and two-question open survey.

held_constant: RQ1 uses the same datasets, train/test splits, and metrics as prior effort-estimation baselines, and baseline code is replicated.
Base and fine-tuned SEEAgent variants share Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; fine-tuning is performed separately per project.
The RQ1 agent is intentionally stripped of multi-agent communication and refinement to match static predictors.
omitted_or_confounded: RQ1 compares fine-tuning and model families, not single-agent versus multi-agent coordination.
RQ2 has no human-only, one-agent, non-specialized-agent, or alternative-model control condition, and it reports perceptions rather than estimation accuracy or convergence quality.
The first author guides sessions as product owner; no blinding, randomization, or independent observer protocol is reported.
The human study uses GPT-4o-mini and in-context examples, whereas RQ1 uses fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B; the two evaluations do not validate the same configuration.
No token, cost, latency, number-of-rounds-to-consensus, or convergence-failure metric is reported.

headline_results.finding: The fine-tuned standalone SEEAgent is best across all three metrics on DM, ME, and US, but not TD. On ME it records MAE 1.217, MMRE 0.414, and PRED(50) 0.747; on US it records 0.350, 0.085, and 1.000.
On TD, SEEAgent records MAE 5.133, MMRE 1.456, and PRED(50) 0.333; its differences from Deep-SE, GPT2SP, and Fine-SE are not significant (p=0.095, 0.359, and 0.524).

Among 12 participants, 66.7% agree agents helped reach consensus, 58.3% say they bridged knowledge gaps, 58.3% identify risk insights, 83.3% find collaboration natural and responses understandable, and all believe SEEAgent could benefit teams. Only one third believe it can substitute for an expert.
The paper attributes collaborative value to role specialization, shared estimates, discussion, and project memory, but no ablation or controlled outcome comparison isolates those mechanisms.

limitations: The multi-agent framework's predictive accuracy is never tested as a multi-agent system.
The human sample is 12 participants on one simplified project, limiting industrial and cross-domain generalization.
The paper describes the human study as rigorous, but the design measures post-session sentiment without a comparator or behavioral ground truth.
The RQ1 projects are highly imbalanced in size; TD has only 73 records and produces the negative result.
Different base models may change both estimation and collaboration behavior, and the modular architecture has not been ablated.
future_work: Run larger commercial studies with diverse developers, domains, and industrial-scale backlogs.
Add source code and infrastructure data to agent knowledge and integrate with Jira or Trello.
Evaluate more LLMs and perform comprehensive component ablations.
Measure rounds to consensus, convergence failure, and response time.
Add voice interaction while preserving auditable communication traces.
combinable_methods: Project-specific fine-tuning when enough historical estimates exist, otherwise in-context retrieval of similar stories.
Role-specific perspectives embedded in a Planning Poker discussion-and-re-estimation protocol.
Structured short-term memory containing the story, conversation, peer estimates, and prior rationale.
Human product-owner arbitration after bounded consensus rounds.
Auditable action and message traces for explaining estimates.

quotes.text: Our evaluation aims to demonstrate the predictive performance of a single SEEAgent against state-of-the-art techniques for agile effort estimation. We also examine how these agents synergise within human teams in a designed environment through a comprehensive human study.
quotes.use: Separates the controlled single-agent accuracy study from the multi-agent human study.

quotes.text: When comparing against the current state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches, SEEAgent fine-tuned outperforms in three out of four projects.
quotes.use: Measured result for the standalone fine-tuned estimator, not the multi-agent system.

quotes.text: Performance in DM and ME projects shows moderate improvements with small to medium effect sizes (0.53 to 0.67), while results in the TD project indicate no significant improvements.
quotes.use: Negative result and effect-size qualification.

quotes.text: While only one third of them thought that the agent can fully substitute an expert (Q9), 75% of the participants did not object to relying on the agent’s estimations (Q10).
quotes.use: Human-study evidence favoring assistance with retained human oversight.

quotes.text: Future work would involve integrating other LLMs, investigating their impact on the performance of our agents in the agile estimation context, and conducting comprehensive ablation studies to validate our modular architecture.
quotes.use: Explicit statement that model effects and architecture components remain unvalidated.

evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Negative and boundary evidence about specialization inside a multi-agent architecture. The experiment compares heterogeneous model constellations with homogeneous model constellations across specialized roles; its phrase 'single LLM across all agents' means one model type reused by multiple agents, not a single-agent system.
evidence_notes.research_design: PathFinder assigns perception/summarization, decision-making, data extraction, and validation to four agents. Mistral-Nemo, Gemma2, and Llama3.1 (4-bit local quantizations) are exhaustively permuted across the first three roles; Gemma2 is fixed as Oracle. All 27 constellations run 10 times on each of four e-commerce sites for one purchase task, totaling 1,080 runs. Temperature is 0.1, Perceptron context is 8K, other contexts are 4K, and execution is capped at 31 steps. One experimenter manually classifies all runs, with ambiguous cases discussed among authors. Outcomes are F1, median steps, and median duration.

held_constant: All 27 assignments of the same three models to the three varied roles are tested on the same task and four sites with ten repeated runs.
Agent architecture, role definitions, local hardware, generation temperature, step cap, and fixed Oracle model are shared across constellations.
Using every permutation permits direct homogeneous-versus-heterogeneous comparisons within PathFinder.
omitted_or_confounded: There is no single-agent architecture baseline, so the experiment cannot estimate the benefit of role decomposition itself.
Gemma2 is fixed as Oracle after pilots because other models terminated early, which removes one role from the factorial comparison and embeds a development-informed choice.
The same prompts are reused across models, but the authors observe model-specific prompt failures and acknowledge prompt bias.
Only one task, four sites, three similarly sized quantized local models, one machine, and one primary human evaluator are included.
The paper reports descriptive F1 differences but no confidence intervals or inferential test for homogeneous versus heterogeneous constellations.

F1 treats the Oracle's success/failure judgment as classification, while true-negative versus false-negative assignment partly depends on expert judgment about whether a timed-out task was theoretically completable.

headline_results.finding: For individual fixed websites, a homogeneous constellation is among the best: Gemma2/Gemma2/Gemma2 reaches F1 0.889 on demo1, Llama/Llama/Llama reaches 0.947 on Ikea, and both reach 0.667 on Netonnet. The authors reject H1 that mixed models outperform on a specific site.

Across sites, Llama3.1/Mistral-Nemo/Mistral-Nemo has the highest average F1 at 0.703, versus 0.660 for homogeneous Gemma2 and 0.654 in Table II for homogeneous Llama3.1. The paper later prints 0.653 for Llama3.1; either way the gain is modest.

Median workload rises with site complexity: 15.0 steps on demo1 and 17.5 on demo2 versus 20.0 on Ikea and 25.0 on Netonnet; the paper gives an example of about 15 minutes on demo1 versus 56 minutes on Netonnet.

A random-forest classifier distinguishes which model produced first-step scene descriptions at over 94% accuracy, led by average length (0.27), noun-to-verb ratio (0.22), and adjective count (0.21). This establishes output-style differences, not that style mismatch causes coordination failures.
The authors propose mutual intelligibility, prompt fit, and site-complexity fit as explanations. They explicitly state that causality cannot be determined from the experiment.

limitations: Homogeneous versus heterogeneous model assignment is not equivalent to single-agent versus multi-agent architecture.
The best cross-site heterogeneous F1 is only 0.043 above homogeneous Gemma2, without uncertainty analysis.
Demo2 has 12 tied top constellations at F1 1.0, so it does not uniquely support homogeneous specialization.
A fixed Gemma2 validator and prompts developed mainly with Gemma2 and Mistral-Nemo can favor particular constellations.
The manual outcome rubric and one-evaluator process leave reliability uncertain despite author discussion of ambiguous cases.
The experiment does not quantify token cost, energy, licensing, maintenance, or production failure behavior.
future_work: Replicate with other multi-agent architectures and broader, stronger model families.
Adapt prompts per model and test whether cross-model response translation improves communication.
Evaluate domain fine-tuning, human-validated retrieval augmentation, and multimodal visual models.
Improve scraping, direct source-data access, and dedicated inference infrastructure for speed and reliability.
Extend beyond one purchase task and four e-commerce sites.
combinable_methods: Exhaustive role-model permutation instead of assuming heterogeneous specialists are complementary.
Repeated runs and explicit step/time measures alongside task effectiveness.
A dedicated validation agent invoked periodically with bounded execution and JSON-repair retries.
Model-specific prompt adaptation or an interface-normalization layer to reduce linguistic mismatch.
Start with one model reused across roles for a known domain, adding heterogeneous models only when cross-domain evidence justifies the maintenance cost.

quotes.text: All permutations were tested on each of the four chosen e-commerce websites and run 10 times with each permutation to acquire robust results. Thereby, 1080 runs were performed in total
quotes.use: Scale and repetition of the factorial role-model experiment.

quotes.text: Thus, we cannot accept Hypothesis H1 (see Section III-3), which proposes that a mixed model approach would outperform the use of a single model across all agents.
quotes.use: Negative finding for heterogeneous model specialization on a fixed site.

evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Strong production and ablation evidence for a role-specialized multi-agent incident-triage system, but weak direct evidence for multi-agent superiority over a matched single LLM agent. The closest causal contrast removes multi-agent negotiation while retaining the surrounding system; all full baselines are classical or deep-learning triage methods with different information sources.
evidence_notes.research_design: Triangle uses Analyzer, Decider, and team-specific Manager agents across semantic distillation, candidate generation, tool-based information enrichment, majority-vote negotiation, and up to five reassignment loops. Evaluation uses 15 months of resolved incidents from large cloud systems: 12 months build historical knowledge and the next 3 months test it. Production impact compares three months before and after deployment for six recently updated services. Offline comparisons use ContentBased, InvertedIndex, LGBM, MART, and DeepCT; nine services test robustness. Ablations remove semantic distillation, multi-agent negotiation, or team information enrichment. A separate public bug-triage evaluation uses 200 assembled cases and semi-manual profiles for 20 developers.

held_constant: Offline methods are evaluated with the same hop-accuracy definition and up to five assignment hops.
Parameters for Triangle and comparison methods are optimized by grid search.
Component ablations share the Triangle pipeline except for the removed mechanism; without negotiation, the Decider assigns directly from ranked candidates.
omitted_or_confounded: No contemporary single-agent or single-prompt LLM is run under the same incident inputs, model, prompts, tools, team documents, information-enrichment access, and hop budget.

DeepCT receives chronological human-enriched discussions while Triangle generates tool-derived enriched discussions, so the strongest baseline comparison changes both architecture and information acquisition.
The exact foundational LLM and its decoding configuration are not specified in the extracted full text.
The production analysis is a before-after comparison without a randomized or contemporaneous control and does not disclose incident counts.
Only resolved incidents are included, creating an outcome-conditioned sample.
The bug-triage transfer study semi-manually constructs team-function analogues, adding human preparation absent from the main automation claim.

headline_results.finding: Across six production services after deployment, reported triage accuracy is 92%, 82%, 96%, 64%, 96%, and 97%; before-after TTE reductions are 18%, 91%, 48%, 72%, 61%, and 67%. Team D's 64% accuracy is a negative result linked by manual inspection to sparse templated descriptions.

Triangle reaches hop-1 accuracy 54.7% and hop-5 accuracy 91.7%, versus DeepCT at 43.4% and 67.6%. Because DeepCT depends on human-enriched discussion while Triangle queries tools to create its own context, this is not an architecture-only comparison.

Removing multi-agent negotiation reduces hop-1/hop-5 accuracy to 42.8%/70.4%; removing information enrichment yields 49.6%/65.8%; removing semantic distillation yields 49.1%/86.1%; the full system yields 54.7%/91.7%. The negotiation ablation supports collaborative decision-making over direct ranking, while enrichment has the largest hop-5 effect.
On 200 MSR 2013 bug cases, Triangle reaches 63.2% accuracy versus DeepCT 52.1%, MART 53.8%, and LGBM 54.8%, after semi-manual developer-profile construction.

The authors attribute gains to specialized knowledge, negotiation, and active external-information collection. The ablations support all three components, but a matched single-agent-with-tools condition is required to isolate whether multiple agents, rather than structured retrieval and iteration, cause the gain.

limitations: No matched single-agent LLM baseline is included despite discussion of single-prompt prior work.
The production deployment is large in data volume (about 600 million logs and more than 20 TB daily), but the number and distribution of evaluated incidents are confidential.
Before-after TTE can be affected by concurrent process, staffing, workload, and service changes that are not controlled in the paper.
Data come from a leading technology company's cloud systems and may not represent other organizations.
Accuracy and TTE omit false-positive rate, recall, calibration, per-incident inference cost, safety of tool queries, and human override rates.
After five failed loops, assignment may involve humans, so the system is not unconditionally autonomous.
future_work: Apply Triangle to a broader range of service systems and organizations.
Add false-positive rate and recall to the evaluation.
Disclose or prospectively measure operational costs, override rates, failures, and drift where confidentiality permits.
Run a matched single-agent LLM with the same retrieval, tools, model, and iteration budget to isolate agent multiplicity.
combinable_methods: Semantic normalization and key-phrase extraction before routing.
Hybrid candidate generation from historical similarity and team-capability documents.
Role-scoped tool access to logs, followed by LLM summarization into traceable evidence.
Majority-vote negotiation with enriched context and bounded reassignment loops.
Documentation standardization and explicit reasoning traces in historical records.
Human escalation after bounded autonomous attempts.

quotes.text: In our offline experiments, T RIANGLE outperforms the state-of-the-art method (DeepCT [4]) by 26%–42% relative improvement in hop accuracy across all hops, achieving up to 91.7% accuracy at hop 5 without relying on manually enriched discussions.
quotes.use: Headline offline result and the important difference in discussion-data dependence.

quotes.text: Notably, Teams C, E, and F achieve outstanding accuracy rates of 96%, 96%, and 97%, respectively. Team A also performs well, with a triage accuracy of 92%. While Team B’s accuracy is slightly lower at 82%, it still reflects a competent level of automated triage. Team D shows a more modest accuracy of 64%.
quotes.use: Production accuracy evidence including the negative service result.

quotes.text: While some may question the absence of more contemporary LLM baselines, we note that prior work [6] has already established through extensive experimentation that GPT-4 significantly outperforms GPT-3.5-Turbo in cloud operation tasks.
quotes.use: Explicit confirmation that a contemporary matched LLM baseline is omitted.

quotes.text: The most substantial performance degradation is observed when the multi-agent negotiation mechanism is removed(w/o MAT). The accuracy drops to 42.8% for Hop 1, which is almost a 12% reduction compared to the full model. The Hop 5 accuracy also sees a significant decline to 70.4%.
quotes.use: Component-level evidence for negotiation over direct Decider ranking.

quotes.text: A common failure mode we observed stemmed from missing or insufficient historical signals—such as lacking indicative keywords—that are essential for associating incidents with the correct team. In other cases, the team documentation itself was vague or ambiguous, making it difficult for the system to derive meaningful mappings.
quotes.use: Observed production limitation and rationale for documentation governance.
